Why hypothetico-deductive rather than deductive-nomological?

I think the 'hypothetico-deductive' classification does a better job of situating exactly what aspects of science are deductive, and these tend not to be deductive in the formal sense. At the same time, it sets out the inductive component of science at the beginning, rather than at the end, so structurally this term does a better job of portraying what science is. All science begins with induction, which leads to the formation of the hypothesis. The only characteristic of the scientific method approaches deductive rigor is that the hypothesis is then tested experimentally, rather the hypothesis is tested as a premise and it's prediction as the conclusion to see if it carries the truth through. By virtue of a great many observations, we deduce that a hypothesis is likely to be true based on it's predictive value. Given this set of boundary conditions, the hypothesis says with a certain % of confidence that X will be the case or we will observe Y.

But this is not the same as formal deduction. It's kind of like quasi-deduction, but that's the reason for calling it hypothetico-deductive, to set out it isn't purely deductive. In other words, we are basically specifying a special type or a special case of deduction specifically for rigorous science. It's like a decoration on the 'deductive' part of the phrase.

My understanding of the term nomological is metaphysical, having to do with the concepts of necessity and possibility. It seems like a contradiction to include both deduction and nomological in the same phrase. Nomological sets out something that is not formally necessary, but appears to be scientifically necessary according to our best natural theories. A good example might be ideal gasses. The ideal gas laws state that a gas' temperature is directly proportional to its pressure and volume, and the crux of being able to define this relationship lawfully as we do, is that it is presided over by the ideal gas constant. We couldn't imagine that this law would not apply anywhere in our universe. But that isn't to say there aren't possible universes where that constant could be different. We'd say it's perfectly logical to imagine a possible world with a different gas law, but nomologically impossible. It's a way of specifying the strength of our possibility criteria. Nomological limits are a lot stronger than logical ones.

We could just say science is nomological and that would be fine. Any "-ology" implies it anyway. I guess we could say hypothetico-deductive and nomological are synonymous in some respects. The former just says more about the method, and the latter is a much better term for talking about possibility.

Suppose we set a piece of warm metal, A, against another piece of metal, B, where B is at the ambient temperature. Let's ignore the presence and effects of air. At what instantaneous temperature (that is, instantaneous rate of change of position of every particle in metal A with respect to time) does the relationship between metal A and B become one in which metal B would, were it able to speak, describe heat as instantiating?

To see why defining/explaining heat is so tricky, we often take the fact of temperature being an average as an elementary fact. Some of the particles in A will be below the average of kinetic energy, while others will be above. If the two metals, A and B, are close enough in temperature, it's quite likely that metal B would be "losing" energy to it's own particles at a rate similar to the energy it is transferring to the particles in A. How do we define heat as a property that could be possessed by something, and which it can spontaneously lose to something which does not have it? What is the heat?

The concept of temperature is a mathematical abstraction. It exists in statistical terms. Where is the heat? It isn't something that we'd say is possessed by one particle, or some property of any single collision of particles. It's a property we accept as an average of still lower properties possessed by many things, namely many particles. But where does heat instantiate? Particularly? It seems that we can reduce heat in terms of an explanation to lower-level facts, which is to say heat just is the cumulative kinetic energy of moving particles, but at the same time there is this nagging sense that this explanation of heat, is not itself heat.

Of course, someone might say that what a conscious thing would call heat is really a matter of quantized sensory information, perhaps we could call it a "sensory package". Heat is what we sense we sense this average differential of heat properties between the summed average of one object's particle's KE, and that same homeostatic value for our sensory thermoceptors. In turn, this just is the explanation of thermoception itself, this sensation that is produced when a receptors state is influenced by some outside stimulus - the feeling of heat, or the sensation of burning or warmth need have no meaningful connection to the properties of heat itself, only to the sensing thing.

There is a fork that develops in how we define heat. On the one hand, heat as a word seems only to be meaningful when we would actually call something heat, and so invokes a certain kind of necessity on the sensory apparatus of a conscious feeler. There could be a real difference in absolute heat between, say, a pencil and a stapler sitting on the same desk, but is 'heat' heat if no living thing would call it heat? On the other hand, there is the idea of heat as a measurable difference in energy, or as the derived function of the rate of change in particle motion with time of the object being "heated".

To see this, suppose metal A raised metal B by just one degree. Would we call this heat? In strict terms, we'd have to, but to see why this creates confusion over the concept, consider a stretch of pavement or concrete (or really any object with decent dimensions). For any average stretch of sidewalk, since temperature is an abstract average entity, there would be localized regions of sidewalk featuring gradients in temperature from still other sub-regions of the sidewalk. If these localized regions vary by even fractions of a degree, on average, does this mean that an object is heating itself? Or does heat only instantiate taking an object as a whole? That is, is the relationship which defines heat only between two separate objects? The concept gets even hairier for a complex fluid system such as the human circulatory system which distributes heat to the tissues.

But the nagging idea stands that we would never call these micro-oscillations heat. And so a person might say, "Well, of course. Because heat is not a micro property, but a macro property. It just is the average of the KE of something, and that was the utility for defining it. It only has meaning when we define the conditions for it to have meaning." But this doesn't reconcile nicely with human language. We all seem to collectively have a distinct mental concept of heat. There is no confusion when we say to someone, "That pan is hot. Don't touch it." We never stop someone cold in the conversation to ask what their boundary conditions are for defining heat.

This seems to imply some kind of threshold for what constitutes heat. Maybe we could unite the intuitive concept of heat with what heat is doing if we were to say, "Heat occurs where a threshold temperature differential exists between two systems, where the subsequent movement toward thermodynamic equilibrium causes a physical deformity in the system whose temperature is being raised." That deformation condition requires definition. We could be generous and call it any observable physical change - but this gets tricky. Deformation in the metals A and B might simply be an expansion along their physical dimensions. Deformation at the level of a human thermoreceptor in the skin might be some protein deformation at the cell membrane causing a signal cascade and an action potential. Does every instance of heat require some sort of physical deformation?

In the case of the human skin, we wouldn't expect every average difference in particulate KE to reach the threshold of sensation. Minor differences, although we can reasonably assume they are real for almost any object sitting at room temperature, wouldn't reach a threshold that would cause an observer to call them heat. We seem to be making the assumption that what receptors are doing is not registering particular discrepancies in particulate energy here or there, but somehow registering average differences in energy between surfaces, namely the one they exist in (the skin) and some external one. Maybe this is algorithmic. The action potential doesn't instantiate unless a certain number of receptors (determined by evolution no doubt) trigger the registration. Evolution might nicely "calibrate" such a mechanism. Something that didn't register sensitively enough would be happy to burn up in a fire. Something that was too sensitive would run from a warm pat of sand.

But now, is heat dependent upon perception? If a formal definition of heat describes something that nobody would call heat, is heat truly reducible to low-level facts. If something can at once meat the criterion for possessing heat according to a finely-tuned instrument, while not meeting any perceptive threshold to be heat, what is heat? Where is it? I'm immediately reminded of the thought experiment usually invoked when discussing the wave-particle duality of quantum objects: "Where is the wave concentrated?" Where is heat?

The reconciliation seems to be a statistical problem. Not every molecular collision will have the properties of an encounter that instantiate heat, only some will. Heat becomes an abstraction about an observer-defined system. Moreover, it is an abstraction about a relationship between two systems that emerges not from any single phenomena, but from a frame of reference which perceives the group of phenomena as a single one. And only in the case that this emerging oneness, which we experience as heat, bears some kind of significance for the perceiving thing. Heat is synthetic. I think it would be better to say that higher-level phenomena have emergent synthetic properties, while they can also possess diffuse lower-level properties.

But it could be the case that we avoid the problem with just another category. We might call heat a secondary property, like the 'solidness' of a cup is a secondary property. Where is the solidness of the cup? Like heat, it doesn't seem to be concentrated at any one molecular relationship, but is an aggregate taken across the whole system that we define as the cup. It becomes a significant property of the cup because we see the cup itself as significant, the cup suggests something to do, something that it does, and so these secondary properties obtain because we have ideas about the object to begin with.

Like heat, solidity also appears to be heterogeneous. I doubt highly that we are sophisticated enough in terms of our materials science that a glass cup, for instance, is perfectly homogeneous in molecular structure. So sub-regions of the cup would have less of the property of solidity than other sub-regions. But for the unit of significance, the property instantiates not in any single or sub-group of molecular bonds, but secondarily for the whole form of the object. We don't speak about the solidity of glass as a class of substance except in the abstract. We speak about the solidity of a glass plate, a glass cup, a glass sheet.

Reductive explanation does not categorically reduce heat in an eliminative way. In the same sense, 'speed' is something categorically different from the frame of reference of an observer, yet it has a universal formal definition involving the function of a rate of change of position over time. A very, very slow rate of change would still possess a speed mathematically, just as a very trivial change in KE across localized regions in a solid object would be an exchange of heat defined within that region, but NEITHER of these reduces the phenomenon of heat or of speed for the class of observers with the sorts of minds like human ones. For humans heat can be unpleasant or painful, or pleasant and even therapeutic. Speed, too, has a relevant range in our forms of experience.

My response to the quote above is referring to the entire section of which it is the final statement. Everything that you have stated here could be the case. But there are two things I'd point out for your consideration:

(1)

Your whole argument (and Acquinas') depends upon arriving at some terminus, whereby backtracking any further, we arrive at a contradiction on causal grounds. This depends upon a causal framework of interpretation, which is itself grounded on properties of time and space. The notion of the problem of an infinite regress of causes only obtains from a primitive conception of time itself, i.e. that reality is a linear, parallel causal series. You have not demonstrated that this is truly the case, except outside of the forms of human experience, that appear to make this the case in order that there should be any experience at all. In other words, the forms of the experience that you have: of events as occurring in time are the result of faculties about your Being which build that experience. It may not be the case that reality is such a distributed collection of linear causal paths.

In general, what you are referring to with all of this is the Cosmological Argument. I think it is a fairly simple one to dispatch with, although not simple to kill completely.*

Destroying the Cosmological Argument

(a) Causal Over-determination

The entire causal framework that the CA rests on is linear causality. The reality is that causality is far more like a web. One paradigm example of this over-determination that has been written about elsewhere is of the sheriff who puts out a bounty on an escaped convict. Two bounty hunters both approaching the convict from opposite sides of a valley might fire a bullet from their rifles at an interval separating them of only minute fractions of a second. To the human observer, the bullets might even appear to strike the head of the convict at the same time. But the second bullet is just a little bit later. What is the cause of the death? In other words, if the effect is death, which bullet was, in fact, the cause? Let's even imagine that we say the first bullet truly is the cause of death, it stands to reason that the effect would STILL HAVE OBTAINED even if the first bullet had never been fired. That is, the effect (death) was OVER-determined in this case. This sort of web of causal relationships makes it difficult to trace clearly defined linear paths of causation back to the first terminus of creation.

(b) There Is No First Cause in the Spatio-Temporal Manifold

Many religious people today considered the Big Bang to be the saving grace of the Cosmological Argument. Here was have an obvious 'beginning'. But they are making a grave error. This, too, was the beginning of time and space. Only if time went back infinitely far before the Big Bang, would the CA hold. However, what we have is a LIMIT, much the same as your old calculus classes, where a function approached zero as a limit, but never actually reached it. A SINGULARITY in the spatio-temporal manifold is an asymptote. Just like in the real number line, a number can keep taking infinitely many steps backward without ever reaching zero as the asymptote, so to in the spatio-temporal manifold, we could keep taking leaps from one event back to its cause, to its cause, to its cause, without ever actually requiring us to acknowledge the singularity. The Big Bang does not sit within a causal series, which is the nature of the singularity.

The one objection to this is perhaps the concept of the Planck scale. It could be possible that reality itself breaks down after going beneath a certain scale length in the spatio-temporal manifold. Theoretically, that boundary exists right now at the Planck length. But this is purely theoretical. There is no evidence that reality does not continue down to infinitely small scale lengths, or in other words, that we couldn't continue to go "into" reality infinitely (if we could become infinitely smaller). But you might consider all of the discoveries being made by the LHC, as far as subatomic particles go. The dictionary of these particles seems to be consistently growing like a set of nested dolls. It isn't clear that we are going to find the "first Particle", which itself might be the scientific equivalent of the religious journey.

(c) Quantifier Switch

I am reminded of a fallacy that is talked about in logic courses, called Quantifier Switch. We'd be committing it if we made the following argument:

Every integer is less than some other integer.

Therefore, there is some integer that is less than all other integers.

Except we know this is not the case. The idea that a series of events could go on infinitely far into the past IS perfectly plausible. The only thing within our body of cosmological theories that works against that possibility is the Big Bang itself. Again, creationists thought it was their saving grace. See (b) above for why it isn't.

(2)

Nothing about your argument for the existence of an uncaused cause suggests that this is necessarily something with personhood, i.e. something which possesses beliefs, intentional states, or basic powers. Tragically for philosophy, and even for the further development of science, Cartesian and other Enlightenment philosophy dominates in the world today, despite being utterly false. Wolfgang Smith has much to say about this issue of bifurcation in his various works.

He points out that ultimately it is just a restatement of Democritean materialism - "by convention there exist colour, the sweet, and the bitter, but in reality only atoms and the void." If one accepts this kind of ridiculous division, then there might be grounds for denying the conventional or traditional (shall I say Aristotelian) concept of time, as "the number of motion". Of course, Democritus and Descartes both have misplaced faith.

It would take much too long to get into the details of Smith's demonstration of the absurdity of bifurcationism, but I will attempt to summarize: there exist in nature corporeal objects X, and functions S, such that there is assigned a corresponding physical object SX. The critical difference between X and SX happens to be that X actually exists. Scholastic philosophy helps to explain this by pointing out that existence is an act, specifically the act of being outside of its causes. Act can be said to perfect a thing according to its nature, while potency is imperfection within a nature. Form determines an essence, but without actualizing a nature with potential it does not actually possess existence. SX can be said to be a mathematical form, while the corporeal object has existence.

Thus the corporeal object X has colour and other qualities, while SX is described exclusively in mathematical terms. Smith points out that the bridge is crossed from X to SX by the theoretician, whereas the bridge from SX to X is crossed by the experimentalist in the act of measurement. Considering this on the quantum level, Heisenberg situated the elementary particles (dare I say primary matter?) "just in the middle between possibility and reality" as "reminiscent of Aristotelian potentiae". What is it that actualizes primary matter? What causes the quantum enigma of the wave function's collapse? The act of measurement itself, which exist on the corporeal, not the physical, plane.

Descartes thus attempts to reduce the res extensa to mere matter, when quantum physics shows us that the existence of objects - elementary matter given existence via an actualizing form - is within and inseparable from the corporeal plane. Bifurcation thus attempts to strip the form, or morphe, from the matter, or hyle, without simultaneously denying an object's existence! The morphe is not contained with the mind of the observer, it is simply real that corporeal interaction is capable of actualizing.

I could go on with this point, but instead I will conclude by referencing James Gibson's landmark The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception, which purports to falsify the Cartesian bifurcationist premise on scientific grounds. I still have yet to read his findings beyond mere summaries - it is on my list - but I can provide just that, a summary, for the time being. Gibson found that what we perceive cannot be reduced to an image - retinal, cerebral, or mental - but instead are what he calls invariants given in ambient light - reflected light from the environment, which is why he argues for an "ecological approach" to visual perception. Wolfgang Smith explains that this "ecological" term is effectively synonymous with what Smith calls "corporeal" - as distinct from the physical. This is sensible, since the implication is that the environment itself possesses not just quantitative, but also qualitative attributes, which are not merely imposed upon it by the mind. In metaphysical terms, therefore, the "invariants" we detect in the act of perception is nothing less than the very form of the objects themselves. If what we are perceiving are indeed forms, and not images, then it is a matter of fact that we are directly perceiving the external world itself, in Smith's terms, "the very forms that constitute reality."

The kind of happiness for which we were made cannot be attained in this life (except by certain extremely blessed saints, and even in their cases it is only glimpses) precisely because our natural end is union with God Himself, He Who is the source of all Being, all Goodness, He in Whom we participate for what being we do have, what good we do have. Therefore, when we think of moments of happiness, and just try to multiply them infinitely, we wonder if that could possibly be enjoyable forever. My reason for saying all this is that, by the time a man reaches heaven, he knows that God is the source of all goodness; he knows that anything other than God is worth literally nothing at all, since all things were created by God from nothing, after all. Such a soul knows what a tremendous gift it was for God to create Him; he knows all the times God gave him the grace that he needed; he knows all the times God forgave him, despite his frequent, almost incessant turnings-away. The soul knows all of this, and as a result the soul wants nothing else but God. This is why, after St. Thomas Aquinas finished his Summa, and presented it to God, kneeling within a church before a crucifix, heard God speak to him: "Thomas, thou hast written well of Me. In the beginning was the Logos, and the Logos was with God, and the Logos is God.

In my thinking about God, I've found that the most challenging set of problems appears to arise when we conceive of God as a person - a being with personhood: something that encounters us personally, with his own beliefs, his own purposes, a discrete experience something like an other mind which set about creation like we imagine a human person does when they set out to paint on a canvas, or build something. This creates for us all sorts of problems, which have been the subjects of many books and many debates.

I consider myself a competent problem solver. One heuristic I've discovered in problem solving that is so obvious, yet so often goes ignored, is this: if it is possible to simplify the more general problem by not introducing more problems in the particulars, you ought to do that. Another way of putting this might be, do not introduce explanations that increase the multiplicity of your problems, or introduce a number of explanations, X, that increase the need for explanations to X^2.

So many problems seem to disappear when we stop taking God to be a person, that my intuition, common sense, and logic all coincide and ring out: "TRUTH!" when I stop to consider the elegance and cleanliness introduced by dispatching with this idea. One reason for that is because there is no analysis of what personhood is that (in my opinion) can escape extremely bounded conditions. Personhood is physical. Personhood becomes in time, and space, in a metaphysical condition of subject-object relationship with reality. There is no meaningful concept of personhood that can escape these terms, or these bounds, which is precisely why we run into trouble with God as person, because we are constantly FORCED to introduce these bounds onto God if we want to take about God meaningfully as a person. Of course, God cannot be omnipresent and omnipotent and perfectly free as something embodied, and therefore we have to extricate him of the very conditions that are the ground for personhood.

Walk with me for a moment. Let's do this as an argument. I want to be very clear about what I'm getting across:

Premises:

(1) Let's assume that what I said in my previous comment, regarding intuitionism is true. That is, human beings do have multiple vectors for ascertaining streams of information that help them to come to true knowledge. Those channels include both the rational, empirical, and irrational (or intuitive). We can call these channels:

(a) - rational

(b) - empirical

(c) - intuitive or "revelatory"

(2) Without a universal blueprint or a visit from the creator, we are in an arbitrary predicament as to deciding which stream of information is best for determining truth.

(3) Knowing the truth ought to do something. Being in the universe, and knowing the truth of that universe, ought to produce some kind of effect.

(4) God created the universe, and therefore is responsible for, and knows fully the truth of that universe.

(5) If human beings are operating according to that truth, some positive effect should be produced. We wouldn't expect that the creator of the universe would deem that knowing the truth of that universe (and operating according to it) would lead to the possessor's destruction. Therefore, knowing truth should produce beneficial effects to the knower. We can call this the Benevolence Criterion.

(6) Many sorts of 'revealed' knowledge exist. That is, there have been many claims made as to the nature of the Truth, each of which has consisted of varying mixtures of (a), (b), and (c). Because (c) cannot be verified epistemologically according to empirical methods, and rationally only by the application of logic, then in cases where two theories containing elements of (c) are not dischargeable empirically, and pure logic is also not clearly able to dispatch either theory, then what remains to prove either theory truer is:

(i) unsubstantiated claims

(ii) some display that one possesses a better theory of truth, by virtue of the effects mentioned in (3) and (5)

Conclusion:

Therefore, by (6)(ii) we could theoretically observe different groups or cultures (taken here as "mass attempts at proving truth"), and analyze the effects of those cultures as the composite of what their wisdom is producing. We can observe the fruits of their truth theories. This would represent perhaps the only verifiable way to say one thing or another about the (c) component of the theories. Again, given (2), there is no stamp of authenticity on the (c) components of a theory, therefore the best way of attempting to know whether the (c) elements of a theory were accurate would be to observe the fruits, the success, the ongoing and perseverative qualities of a culture across time: the wisdom and art it produces.

By this argument, I believe we do have a reasonable means of saying that not all theories about ultimate reality are equally good.

But if we are to justify our claimed knowledge on the basis of anything more than man's personal claims that such and such a theory is better, we require MORE THAN said claim, otherwise this is circular, and illogical - which causes the (c) components of that theory to become less rationally justifiable according to (2) and (6), making it a less viable theory.

Therefore, there is no univocal way, by claims alone, to say with certainty that your theory is the only true theory of reality. No authoritative text or measure of follower-ship could do this. We could further justify a theory of reality by looking at what it does to a society across time, BUT it remains that we cannot do as you have done and merely state that one theory is the truth and all others are man-made, else you compromise and logically weaken your own theory.

Furthermore:

Let's now imagine that we have multiple societies which have persevered through time with competing theories of truth. Both have had various failures and successes, both have been pockmarked by history. One society thrives in certain areas, and the second thrives in areas where the first does not. We could make myriad claims about which society is better, but largely we classify these as subjective claims of value because it stands that: both societies are still here and doing what they do, unbroken.

What should we do about analyzing the (c) components of their theories?

It seems clear to me that the most logical thing we could do, would be to study both of the society's theories and look for COMMON ATTRIBUTES. We may even have the strong belief that one of the theories is the right one, but again, by the conclusion of our argument above, we cannot make a certainty claim about that. Even in the case that we believe our theory is the right one, we'd still be remiss to sit back on our heels with the illusion of certainty, and not look for common threads between both society's theories.

Understanding that we cannot make a certainty claim would cause the logical person to say: "Both of these societies have lasted. Given the effects we mentioned in (5) with our Benevolence Criterion, it suggests BOTH of these societies are at least doing some things right." I should, therefore, analyze what aspects of their two theories are common to each other, and by doing this I might identify which candidate aspects of the theories are responsible for both society's continuity and thriving. THAT should most likely lead me to a stronger theory of truth than dismissing one, or the other, theory. In other words, what we are after is a synthesis.

This entails that certain particulars of either theory may not transmit to the synthesis. This does not indicate that, in the end, we must abandon things like our particular religious story, or names, or events therein, but IN ORDER TO appreciate and perform the synthesis, we must put those on standby. What results from the synthesis has the potential, if not to eliminate names or discrete events from our theory, at least to compel us to perhaps remodel aspects of our theory if we find ourselves compelled to do so. This synthetic process DOES NOT suggest that we treat all theories equally. If you follow the logic, that should be clear.

Nor does it suggest that we actually instantiate a third theory based on the synthesis. But it does suggest that the logical person and the logical society would remain open to an ongoing potential for remodeling. That remodeling process can occur at two levels: within the individual who is doing the observing and thinking, and with the society itself that as a collective commits itself to this foregoing process as a statement of it's commitment to seeking truth.

The above argument, conclusion, and discussion encapsulate what I take to be mysticism, and it should logically maximize the (a), (b), and (c) aspects of our theories of reality. By extension, faith by itself is inferior to the mystical process I have just described.

Aquinas argues thus (I Q19 A9):

Reply to Objection 1. Some have said that although God does not will evil, yet He wills that evil should be or be done, because, although evil is not a good, yet it is good that evil should be or be done. Reply to Objection 2. Evil does not operate towards the perfection and beauty of the universe, except accidentally, as said above (Reply to Objection 1). Therefore Dionysius in saying that "evil would conduce to the perfection of the universe," draws a conclusion by reduction to an absurdity.

Aquinas, in his fourth proof (I Q2 A3), writes:

The fourth way is taken from the gradation to be found in things. Among beings there are some more and some less good, true, noble and the like. But "more" and "less" are predicated of different things, according as they resemble in their different ways something which is the maximum, as a thing is said to be hotter according as it more nearly resembles that which is hottest; so that there is something which is truest, something best, something noblest and, consequently, something which is uttermost being; for those things that are greatest in truth are greatest in being, as it is written in Metaph. ii. Now the maximum in any genus is the cause of all in that genus; as fire, which is the maximum heat, is the cause of all hot things. Therefore there must also be something which is to all beings the cause of their being, goodness, and every other perfection; and this we call God.

Now, one can dodge the consequences of this proof if one rejects the actual existence of goodness, nobility, love, and the like - at least if these are rejected as being transcendent, but merely images or illusions built by the mind. But to believe this is a faith as much as to believe the contrary.

Thus, if we accept the real transcendent reality of things such as love, it follows from this proof that such an effect can only proceed from a greater cause. Therefore in the ultimate reality there must be love. But for this to be the case He must be a person (speaking analogically, since, as with all descriptions of God, equivocal and univocal descriptions are impossible). The same conclusion follows from Aquinas' fifth proof with regard to intelligence and order in the universe, that it must be intelligently ordered and directed to some end - thus requiring the ultimate reality to have something analogous to personhood.

Aquinas' reply to the final objection in the first Article I cited above runs thus:

Reply to Objection 3. The statements that evil exists, and that evil exists not, are opposed as contradictories; yet the statements that anyone wills evil to exist and that he wills it not to be, are not so opposed; since either is affirmative. God therefore neither wills evil to be done, nor wills it not to be done, but wills to permit evil to be done; and this is a good.

So it is neither a case of God positively willing or not willing evil itself. As I understand it, this conclusion is inseparable from the proper understanding of evil as non-being, as not actually existing, except as being a privation of a good, which actually exists. God does not will something that isn't to be; though He does permit the "presence" of this isn't insofar as it represents a lesser good than could be within a specific nature for the sake of a greater good that results. In this way the evil is only accidental to the effect, which means it bears no causal connection to the effect, since causation is based on essentials. Therefore evil is not made necessary for this greater good; God simply permitted a lesser good than could be. This is what he meant above when saying that evil is not permitted for the sake of the perfection of the universe, except accidentally. Really what is permitted for the sake of the perfection of the universe is that things be less good than they could be, so that the whole can be perfected.

I have quoted the Summa Theologica enough; now for the Summa Contra Gentiles, in response to the first objection:

If, however, we consider the divine ordinance whereby God decided by His intellect and will to bring things into being, then the production of things proceeds from the necessity of divine ordinance: for it is impossible that God should decide to do a certain thing which afterwards He did not, otherwise His decision would be either changeable or weak.

In other words, that free agents, which God might create, will knowably sin cannot be a determinate of whether God creates them or not, since this would make God's creation and will contingent upon the actions of creatures yet uncreated. Thus it is a logical impossibility for the sin of man to possibly be an antecedent to God's creation. It bears on Him nought. By man's own natural power (before the Fall) he could have made the universe one without sin - but given that God decided to create free will, it was up to man and not Him to prevent sin.

This is all understood in the context that creation is not necessary, that God was not compelled to create, let alone a specific creation. There was nothing prior to God requiring that He create a universe without evil. There was nothing due to the creatures in way of being. This leads us to the second objection, of why, then, create at all, if a universe containing evil proves to be unnecessary (in that, a universe without evil could have been, or no universe at all).

And the primary answer is that God did not create for the sake of the creation, but in order to manifest His own supreme goodness; He is His own object for creation (the alpha and omega). God is pleased with the reflection of Himself in creation, and this pleasure is the sufficient reason for the existence of the universe, and by extension it is the sufficient reason for the existence of the moral evil within this universe that was created. It can further be argued that, by creating a universe in which sin is permitted - not willed - God is able to manifest His goodness in ways not otherwise possible - like the fullness of His justice, or even more so, His mercy. This ties into the point I made with Chiro, that a story with conflict is more interesting to man than a story without conflict. Well, in an analogous sense, this may be true with God. Acknowledging that creation was made for His sake above all - for Love of Himself and His own goodness - we can better understand how a universe in which His goodness is all the more starkly manifest would be more pleasing to God than any other - like one without free will, or no universe at all - and again, it is the pleasure of God that is the supreme motive for all action.

Eventually we necessarily reach a limit to speculation or apprehension of these matters. We simply cannot understand exactly and with rational certainly why this universe was made and not any other. Eventually we reach a point so beyond speculation, as I have repeatedly insisted, that we depend on faith. The theist can no more conceive of an ultimate reason for this particular creation than the atheist can explain the ultimate cause for the order of the universe - without unjustifiably doing away with the ultimate causation itself.
